anchors.quote: No replacement computation or quantum candidate is retained, so there is no proposed quantum input domain, state, traversal, update rule, termination rule, or decoding procedure to place in plan; plan is therefore null. The existing computation remains classical. In solve mode, program.py lines 22-27 call kernel.solve(matrix, rhs), compute the proposed residual, preserve variable order when constructing the named proposal and deltas, and compare the scaled diagnostic with residual_limit. kernel.py lines 9-26 initialize an augmented mutable copy rows = [matrix row plus rhs value]. For each column col from 0 through n-1, they inspect row indices col through n-1, select the row maximizing abs(rows[i][col]) with Python max's first-index tie behavior, reject an exactly zero selected pivot, swap it into row col, and eliminate every lower row by computing factor = rows[i][col] / rows[col][col] and updating entries j from col through n inclusive in ascending order. After elimination, back substitution initializes x to n zeros, traverses i from n-1 down to 0, and computes x[i] from the augmented value minus the ascending generator sum over already computed x[j], divided by the diagonal. It terminates by rejecting any nonfinite solution value or returning x; n = 0 naturally returns an empty vector. kernel.py lines 29-38 compute each residual component as the ordered row dot product minus rhs, then the infinity norm, matrix infinity norm, denominator, overflow checks, and the specified zero-denominator rule. These routines depend on validated finite binary64 matrix, rhs, current, distinct variable names, mode, and limit; solve activates only when mode is solve, while residual activates before the mode branch and again for a proposal. Validation, inspect behavior, exact-zero singularity rejection, detected-overflow rejection, operation ordering, first-pivot tie handling, output ordering, and nonmutation must remain intact. Admission to a Grover-style replacement would require a justified finite candidate domain, a pure reversible predicate, deterministic-equivalent success and no-solution handling, and accounted encoding and oracle resources. Admission to QUBO/Ising would require a justified binary encoding, explicit objective coefficients and constraints, sufficient penalty bounds, exact decoding, and proof that the required solution and failure semantics are preserved. None is supplied. Outside those admission conditions, including this case, behavior remains the stated classical implementation. The HPL attribution supports only the classical algorithmic context; this is explicitly not a compliant HPL performance run, and no quantum workload, hardware, resource, benchmark, or advantage evidence is supplied.
